scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

So, the person is married, and their wife's parents paid for most of the wedding. After the wedding, the parents seemed fine, but the next morning, they were upset, saying they felt spiritually assaulted and thought the couple did it on purpose. They wanted to discuss it later but then demanded that the couple have their ceremony blessed by their pastor. The couple tried to compromise by doing it where they live, but the parents insisted it be done at their house. They also sent a message saying "honor thy mother and father" and made their gift conditional on this blessing. The couple is now considering recording the blessing where they live and sending it, but they're also considering refusing the gift and reducing contact if the parents aren't satisfied.

The question is whether the couple's actions are morally acceptable.

First, I need to identify the key actions and the moral principles involved. The couple agreed to include a religious element in their ceremony because the parents paid for it, even though they're non-religious. They requested the officiant to include it, but it didn't happen. Then, when the parents got upset, the couple tried to compromise by agreeing to have a blessing, but the parents were still upset and made the gift conditional.

So, the main actions are:

1. Agreeing to include a religious element in the ceremony to please the parents who paid for the wedding.
2. Trying to compromise by agreeing to have a blessing where they live.
3. Considering refusing the gift and reducing contact if the parents aren't satisfied.

Now, I need to evaluate these actions based on moral principles. Some relevant principles might include honesty, respect for others' beliefs, fairness, and the importance of family relationships.

First, the couple agreed to include a religious element they didn't believe in to avoid conflict and because the parents paid for the wedding. This could be seen as a form of deception or compromise. On one hand, they were trying to maintain a good relationship with their in-laws and avoid conflict. On the other hand, they were going against their own beliefs, which could be seen as dishonest or compromising their integrity.

Second, when the parents got upset, the couple tried to compromise by agreeing to have a blessing where they live. This shows an attempt to meet the parents halfway and maintain peace. However, the parents were still insistent on having it done at their house, which the couple refused. This could be seen as standing their ground or being inflexible.

Third, the couple is considering refusing the gift and reducing contact if the parents aren't satisfied. This could be seen as a way to assert their independence and set boundaries, but it could also be seen as ungrateful or hurtful to the parents who paid for the wedding.

Now, I need to weigh these actions against the moral principles. 

Honesty: The couple didn't fully represent their beliefs by agreeing to include a religious element. This could be seen as dishonest because they were pretending to be religious to please their in-laws.

Respect for others' beliefs: While the couple didn't agree with the parents' religious beliefs, they tried to accommodate them by including a prayer and blessing. However, the parents took offense even though the officiant didn't include the religious elements, which complicates things.

Fairness: The parents paid for the wedding, so they might feel entitled to have some say in the ceremony. However, the couple's beliefs should also be respected.

Family relationships: The couple is trying to maintain a good relationship with their in-laws but is also standing up for their own beliefs. This balance is tricky.

Considering all this, the couple's actions involve some compromise and attempts to maintain peace, but they also involve going against their own beliefs and potentially causing hurt feelings. The decision to refuse the gift and reduce contact if the parents aren't satisfied could be seen as a way to assert their independence but might also be seen as ungrateful.

Overall, while the couple's intentions to maintain peace and respect their in-laws' contributions are commendable, their compromise on their own beliefs and the potential for causing further conflict by refusing the gift and reducing contact could be seen as morally complex. However, given that they tried to compromise and only considered refusing the gift as a last resort, their actions might still be considered morally acceptable.
